content: The results obtained by the polio-accredited laboratory must be reported and uploaded to the database immediately. The laboratory is responsible for ensuring that these results are shared with the national program in a timely and comprehensive manner. Additionally, the laboratory must assist in interpreting the findings and their significance. The flow of information should adhere to the standard system outlined in the relevant guidelines. Effective data management involves the efficient collection, transfer, and storage of data. Data can be recorded either manually or electronically using prescribed forms. Options for data entry include MS Access databases, Excel templates, or direct entry into ODK. Information may also be shared globally through the Polio Information System. Countries are encouraged to collaborate with WHO regional offices to adopt fully electronic systems for data collection and reporting, incorporating standardized variables used in national, regional, and global databases. Performance indicators for environmental surveillance include the sensitivity of the network, timeliness of sample collection, adequacy of samples, and timeliness of sample shipment. Samples arriving at WHO-accredited laboratories in good condition should exceed 80%, with good condition defined as a volume greater than 1 liter, maintenance of the reverse cold chain, and no leakage. Samples should also arrive at the laboratory within three days (national) or seven days (international) of collection. The timeliness of laboratory reporting is critical, with preliminary results (e.g., presence of poliovirus) expected within 14 days, intratypic differentiation (ITD) results within seven days, and sequencing results within 14 days. Periodic evaluations of environmental sites and networks should be conducted, ideally integrated with acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) surveillance reviews. WHO and GPEI staff can support analysis and field assessments. Site evaluations should trigger corrective actions if necessary, such as validating new sites, monitoring existing sites, or discontinuing sites with persistently low enterovirus isolation rates. When wild poliovirus (WPV) or vaccine-derived poliovirus (VDPV) is detected in the environment, follow-up investigations must determine the significance of the findings. The response depends on factors such as the country’s polio-free status, history of VDPV outbreaks, immunization coverage, quality of AFP surveillance, and the specific goal of environmental surveillance. In polio-endemic or recently endemic areas, detection of WPV or VDPV should prompt targeted improvements in surveillance and immunization. In polio-free countries, such detection represents a public health emergency requiring immediate investigation. Programmatic actions in response to WPV or VDPV detection include rapid communication with all reporting units within 24 hours, heightened active surveillance for AFP cases, and notification of WHO within 48 hours. Enhanced environmental sampling may be necessary to increase the sensitivity of virus detection, and additional sampling sites may be investigated. Routine surveillance data should be reviewed to identify any missed polio cases, and active case searches should be conducted in the community. Immunization coverage should be assessed, and preliminary planning for an immunization response should begin, considering the type of vaccine to be used (e.g., OPV, IPV, or both). For individuals with primary immunodeficiency disorders (PIDs), prolonged poliovirus shedding can lead to the emergence of immunodeficiency-related vaccine-derived polioviruses (iVDPVs). Surveillance aims to identify PID patients excreting poliovirus before they develop paralysis or initiate community transmission. Case management protocols and public health responses should reduce the risk of poliovirus transmission and prevent adverse outcomes. PID patients at risk of poliovirus excretion are defined as those with primary antibody or combined humoral and cellular immunodeficiency disorders, confirmed by low immunoglobulin levels for their age. Surveillance systems should identify previously diagnosed PID patients through national and facility registries and screen newly diagnosed PID patients for poliovirus excretion. Stool specimens from PID patients should be tested for poliovirus, and follow-up testing should be conducted monthly for those with positive specimens and annually for those with negative specimens. Detailed investigations should assess the risk of poliovirus circulation in the community and initiate case management and public health responses. Close contacts of PID patients shedding poliovirus should have their vaccination status determined, and stool samples may be collected for testing. Community surveys should assess polio vaccination coverage and risk factors for fecal-oral transmission, such as high population density and inadequate sanitation. Public health responses depend on the type of poliovirus isolated, sequencing data, and community transmission risk factors. Treatment with antiviral drugs may be considered for PID patients excreting VDPV, shedding Sabin strains for more than two months, or excreting WPV. Antivirals are not indicated for contacts potentially exposed to poliovirus. Surveillance data are essential for detecting and monitoring PID patients with prolonged poliovirus excretion, preventing paralysis and other adverse outcomes, and recording the number and location of poliovirus excretors. Data sources include case investigation forms, follow-up forms, and PID patient registries. Epidemiological analysis should include the number of PID patients at risk of poliovirus excretion, the duration of Sabin excretion, and the geographic distribution of excretors.
